qs.q: A 16-year-old patient complains of severe bone pain in the proximal tibia that occurs predominantly at night and is dramatically relieved by aspirin. A small lesion under 2 cm is identified. What is the primary reason this tumour responds so well to aspirin?
o: The tumor lacks the calcification typically seen in osteoblastomas
The tumor produces prostaglandins that aspirin effectively inhibits
The tumor shows a t(11;22) translocation that NSAIDs block
The tumor carries a GNAS mutation leading to increased osteoclast activity
qs.e: Osteoid osteomas produce prostaglandins, which cause severe night pain and are effectively blocked by aspirin. Larger osteoblastomas do not share this dramatic pain relief response to aspirin despite being in the same tumour family.

qs.q: During arthroscopic knee surgery, a surgeon examines the tibial plateau attachments. Which structure attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia?
qs.e: The anterior cruciate ligament attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia. The posterior cruciate ligament attaches to the posterior intercondylar area.

qs.q: The 'screw-home' mechanism of the knee joint involves passive medial rotation of the femur on the tibia during terminal extension. This mechanism causes tightening of which primary ligament, contributing to knee stability?
qs.e: The screw-home mechanism tightens both the collateral and cruciate ligaments, but the tibial (medial) collateral ligament is particularly important in resisting external rotation and providing stability in full extension, along with the anterior cruciate ligament. The question asks for a primary ligament that becomes tight due to the mechanism, and the MCL is a strong contributor to full extension stability.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The tibia is the main weight‑bearing bone of the lower leg, forming the knee and ankle joints. Its shape, blood supply and nerve innervation are key to diagnosing fractures, infections and vascular problems.

sections.p: The tibia is the larger of the two bones in the lower leg, running from the knee to the ankle. It supports most of the body weight and provides attachment sites for major muscles and ligaments.

The tibia has a proximal metaphysis, a shaft, and a distal metaphysis ending in the medial and lateral condyles. The proximal end articulates with the femur and patella; the distal end with the talus and fibula.

t.b: Detects fractures, alignment, and bone density; a displaced fracture indicates need for surgical fixation.

sections.p: Anteriorly lies the patellar tendon and quadriceps; posteriorly the popliteal artery and vein. Medially the medial collateral ligament and meniscus attach; laterally the lateral collateral ligament.

t.b: Assesses soft tissue injuries around the tibia; a thickened medial collateral ligament suggests sprain.

sections.p: The tibial artery, a branch of the popliteal artery, supplies the shaft and metaphysis. The nutrient artery enters the bone via the tibial tuberosity.

t.b: Shows arterial occlusion or aneurysm; a filling defect indicates thrombus.

sections.p: The anterior tibial nerve supplies the anterior compartment; the tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment. Sensory branches run along the medial and lateral borders.

t.b: Detects neuropathy; slowed conduction suggests compressive injury.

sections.p: The tibia bears weight, facilitates locomotion, and provides a lever for muscle action. It also protects neurovascular structures in the leg.

t.b: Identifies abnormal loading patterns; a limp may indicate tibial stress fracture.

sections.p: Fractures, osteomyelitis, tibial plateau lesions, and osteoid osteoma are common. In low‑resource settings, infections and delayed fracture healing are major concerns.

t.b: Initial assessment of fracture type and displacement; a displaced fracture needs reduction.

faq.q: What is the tibial tuberosity used for?
faq.a: It is the insertion of the patellar tendon and a landmark for procedures like osteoid osteoma biopsy.

faq.q: How does a tibial fracture heal?
faq.a: It heals by callus formation; adequate alignment and stability are essential for proper remodeling.

faq.q: Why is the tibia called the shinbone?
faq.a: Because it forms the prominent bone on the front of the lower leg, visible as the shin.
